title: Data Definition Language (DDL)
relevance: SDE interviews and OAs test whether candidates can define schemas safely, enforce integrity with constraints, and distinguish DDL operations like TRUNCATE, DROP, and ALTER from row-level DML.

phases.goal: Establish that DDL defines schema structure and that constraints actively reject invalid data.

must_hit.point: DDL commands define, modify, and destroy database object structure (tables, views, indexes, schemas), not the row data itself.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says DDL is about the blueprint/schema of objects rather than inserting or updating business rows.

must_hit.point: CREATE TABLE creates a new empty table; integrity rules are enforced via constraints that reject violating INSERT or UPDATE operations entirely.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions empty table creation plus constraints as guardians that fail the whole statement on violation.

must_hit.point: PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each row and is equivalent to UNIQUE plus NOT NULL; a table can have at most one primary key.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States uniqueness, non-nullness, and the single-primary-key limit.

must_hit.point: UNIQUE allows multiple unique columns and can often accept multiple nulls because null is not equal to null; NOT NULL forbids empty values; CHECK enforces a logical condition; REFERENCES is an inline foreign key; DEFAULT supplies a fallback when a value is omitted.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists several column constraints with the UNIQUE-null nuance and DEFAULT as fallback rather than validation.

probes: What is DDL, and how do PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, and foreign-key constraints protect data when you create a table?

hints.1: Think schema blueprint versus the data stored in rows.
hints.2: Walk column constraints: identity of a row, nullability, uniqueness, predicates, parent references, and defaults.
hints.3: DDL shapes tables/views/indexes; PRIMARY KEY = UNIQUE + NOT NULL (one per table); UNIQUE may allow multiple nulls; violations fail the whole INSERT/UPDATE.

phases.goal: Explain how table-level constraints, referential actions, views, indexes, ALTER, and identity columns actually work.

must_hit.point: Table-level constraints are declared after columns when rules span multiple columns or need explicit names (composite PRIMARY KEY, named FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, UNIQUE).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes CONSTRAINT ... after column list for composite keys and named FKs/checks.

must_hit.point: Foreign-key referential actions control parent delete/update: RESTRICT blocks immediately if children exist (default); NO ACTION is similar but deferred to transaction end; CASCADE deletes/updates matching children; SET NULL blanks the child FK; SET DEFAULT applies the child's DEFAULT.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the five actions and contrasts immediate RESTRICT vs deferred NO ACTION vs CASCADE/SET NULL/SET DEFAULT.

must_hit.point: A view stores the query, not the data; querying it runs the stored query against live base tables. Materialized views store a physical snapshot and need manual refresh (e.g. REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY) because they go stale when base tables change.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts virtual stored query vs on-disk snapshot plus explicit refresh.

must_hit.point: Updatable views in simple one-to-one cases (single base table, no GROUP BY, JOINs, or DISTINCT) allow UPDATE/INSERT that pass through to the underlying table.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the simplicity conditions and that modifications hit the base table.

must_hit.point: Indexes (usually B-Tree) avoid sequential full-table scans; types include unique, composite (column order matters), and partial indexes; ALTER TABLE can add/drop/rename columns, change types, and add/drop constraints or defaults without dropping the table.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions B-Tree/scan avoidance plus at least composite/partial and several ALTER forms.

must_hit.point: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY prevents manual ID inserts; SERIAL still allows override and can desynchronize the sequence. Generated columns in PostgreSQL are STORED (written to disk). Temporary tables exist only for the current session and vanish on disconnect; CTAS creates and populates a table from a SELECT.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts IDENTITY vs SERIAL, STORED generated columns, session-scoped temps, and CTAS snapshotting.

probes: If a parent row is deleted, what do ON DELETE CASCADE, RESTRICT, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT, and NO ACTION do—and how do views, indexes, and ALTER TABLE fit into DDL mechanics?

hints.1: Start from what happens to child rows when the parent changes.
hints.2: Cover named/composite constraints, the five referential actions, view vs materialized view, then index/ALTER basics.
hints.3: RESTRICT blocks now; NO ACTION checks at commit; CASCADE follows children; SET NULL/DEFAULT rewrite FKs; views store queries; materialized views need REFRESH; indexes are usually B-Trees; ALTER evolves structure in place.

phases.goal: Surface the read/write, freshness, and safety tradeoffs the file emphasizes for indexes, views, CASCADE, and deletion commands.

must_hit.point: Indexes speed reads but every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also maintain the index, so over-indexing slows writes.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly pairs faster reads with slower DML from index maintenance.

must_hit.point: Regular views always see live data; materialized views are fast because precomputed but become stale until manually refreshed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Freshness vs speed tradeoff with mandatory refresh called out.

must_hit.point: OVERUSING ON DELETE CASCADE risks catastrophic cascading deletes across related tables; RESTRICT is the safer default for critical data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Warns about silent mass deletion and prefers RESTRICT for critical data.

must_hit.point: TRUNCATE empties a table at storage-page level (DDL) keeping structure; DELETE removes rows one-by-one with full logging and trigger firing; DROP destroys structure and data.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates structure retention, logging/triggers, and total object destruction.

probes: Compare indexing and materialized views for performance versus freshness/write cost, and when would you choose RESTRICT over CASCADE or TRUNCATE over DELETE?

hints.1: Every speedup here has a maintenance or safety cost.
hints.2: Index write amplification; matview staleness; CASCADE blast radius; TRUNCATE vs row-logged DELETE.
hints.3: More indexes → faster reads, slower writes; matviews need REFRESH; CASCADE can wipe dependents—prefer RESTRICT; TRUNCATE deallocates pages and skips ON DELETE triggers, DELETE logs and fires them.

phases.goal: Apply DDL choices to real schema and cleanup scenarios without mixing up DROP, TRUNCATE, and DELETE.

must_hit.point: Use views to hide complex JOINs and to grant access to a column/row subset (e.g. exclude salary) without exposing the base table.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives simplicity and security use cases for CREATE VIEW.

must_hit.point: Choose referential actions deliberately: RESTRICT/NO ACTION to protect parents with children; CASCADE only when child rows should disappear with the parent; SET NULL when orphaning via null FK is acceptable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps business intent to a specific ON DELETE/ON UPDATE action.

must_hit.point: For bulk emptying while keeping the table, prefer TRUNCATE (optionally RESTART IDENTITY); use DELETE when you need WHERE filters, full logging, or ON DELETE triggers; use DROP (optionally CASCADE) only when the object itself should go.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Picks the right removal command for structure retention, selective delete, or full destroy.

must_hit.point: Use CTAS to snapshot query results into a physical table for analytics; use TEMPORARY tables as session-scoped scratchpads that other connections cannot see.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names CTAS for snapshots and temp tables for session-local work.

probes: You need a secure employee listing without salaries, a safe FK delete policy, and a way to clear a huge logs table—what DDL would you write and why?

hints.1: Match the tool to the goal: projection, referential policy, or mass clear.
hints.2: View for restricted columns; ON DELETE choice for parent/child; TRUNCATE/DELETE/DROP for cleanup.
hints.3: CREATE VIEW without salary; default RESTRICT unless children should go; TRUNCATE for fast full clear (no ON DELETE triggers), DELETE for filtered/trigger-aware removal, DROP to remove the table.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Indexes (typically B-Tree) avoid sequential scans and speed lookups, but every insert/update/delete must update the indexes too, so over-indexing speeds reads while severely slowing writes.

A regular view stores only the query and always returns live base-table data; a materialized view stores a precomputed snapshot for fast reads but goes stale until you manually REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW (CONCURRENTLY in the example).

CASCADE automatically deletes matching child rows with the parent, which can silently wipe departments, employees, and audit logs; RESTRICT blocks parent deletion when children exist and is the safer default for critical data.

DROP destroys table structure and data; DELETE removes rows one-by-one with full logging and fires triggers (and can use WHERE); TRUNCATE is DDL that deallocates data pages, keeps structure, is minimally logged, cannot activate ON DELETE triggers, and in PostgreSQL is fully transactional with ROLLBACK restoring data.

tradeoffs.topic: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY vs SERIAL
tradeoffs.strong_answer: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY blocks manual ID inserts; SERIAL still allows override, which can desynchronize the sequence.

gotchas.trap: Treating UNIQUE like PRIMARY KEY regarding nulls
gotchas.correction: UNIQUE can often accept multiple null values because null is not equal to null; PRIMARY KEY implies NOT NULL as well.

gotchas.trap: Defaulting every foreign key to ON DELETE CASCADE
gotchas.correction: CASCADE can cascade through departments, employees, and audit logs and delete an organization's data in milliseconds; use RESTRICT by default for critical data.

gotchas.trap: Assuming TRUNCATE behaves like DELETE for triggers and categorization
gotchas.correction: TRUNCATE is DDL operating at storage/page level; it cannot activate ON DELETE triggers, so audit-on-delete logic will not run.

gotchas.trap: Assuming TRUNCATE cannot be rolled back
gotchas.correction: In PostgreSQL, TRUNCATE inside a transaction can be ROLLBACKed and the data is restored.

gotchas.trap: Expecting a temporary table to be visible from another connection
gotchas.correction: TEMPORARY tables exist only for the current session; another connection or terminal will not see them.

gotchas.trap: Expecting a materialized view to stay current automatically
gotchas.correction: Base-table changes do not update the materialized snapshot; you must run REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW (CONCURRENTLY in the example).
Only simple views mapping one-to-one to a single base table without GROUP BY, JOINs, or DISTINCT are updatable in PostgreSQL.
For multi-column indexes, column order matters heavily for how the query optimizer can use the index.
